o: Support fix/unfix of single bits, flip of all bits, and all/one/count/toString queries with up to 1e5 operations on up to 1e5 bits. The naive design stores the literal bit string and rebuilds it on flip — O(size) per flip, which can degrade to O(size * flips). The lazy design keeps a stored string plus a 'flipped' flag: flip is O(1) (toggle the flag), fix/unfix consult the effective bit (stored bit XOR flag), and only toString materializes the inversion (allowed at most 5 times).
k: Lazy flipping: represent flip as a boolean flag instead of touching every bit.
Effective bit at i = stored[i] XOR flag; count of ones updates incrementally in fix/unfix and complementarily on flip.

a.i: Keep the actual bits in a mutable array and maintain the popcount; flip rewrites every character.
s: Store a char array and an integer count of ones.
fix/unfix adjust one cell and the count; flip rewrites all cells and sets count = size - count.
Queries read the count; toString joins the array.
a.t: O(size) per flip, O(1) otherwise — fine given the call limits but degradable

a.i: Store bits that may be logically inverted by a flag; flip toggles the flag in O(1), and only toString pays to materialize the true bits.
s: Keep char array b, flag f, count c of effective ones.
fix: if effective bit is 0, set b[idx] to the character representing effective 1 and c++.
unfix mirrors it; flip toggles f and sets c = size - c.
toString emits b, inverted if f.
a.t: O(1) for everything except toString, which is O(size) and limited to 5 calls

w: Present the lazy-flag design as the main answer; it makes flip O(1), which matters if flips dominate. Pitfalls: getting the effective-bit polarity backwards in fix/unfix, and remembering count complements on flip. Follow-up: support range flips with a difference array, or pack bits into integers for memory efficiency.
